lesson.title: Choosing between paths

steps.headline: A condition is a test with a true or false answer, and the answer decides which branch of a program runs.

lead.text: The till rule becomes a program once the bill is replaced by x. In the figure the first line stores 8 in x, and the line if x > 5: is the test. It asks whether x is greater than 5, a question that can be answered only by *true* or *false*, and a test of this kind is called a **condition**.

The lines beneath it are indented by four spaces, and the indentation is what marks them as belonging to the test. The indented lines straight after the if line form one **branch**, which runs only when the condition is true. The line else: begins the other branch, which runs only when the condition is false, so *exactly one* of the two branches runs each time and the other is skipped.

afterFigure.text: Here x holds 8, and 8 > 5 is true, so the first branch runs and x becomes 18. Had x held 3 instead, the condition would have been false, the else branch would have run, and x would have become 2. Run the code and step through it with the trace control to see the test line appear as a step of its own before either branch begins.

lead.text: Apply the till rule from the opening, which takes £4 off any bill over £30, to a bill that sits exactly on the limit.

reveal.text: A program has to make the same choice, and the next screen shows how it says which of the two readings it means.

steps.headline: A test can include its boundary value or leave it out, and one symbol decides which.

lead.text: Every test of this kind has a place where its answer changes. For x > 5 that place is 5, and the symbol > means *strictly* greater, so 5 itself fails the test, exactly as a bill of £30 fails “over £30”. Writing >= instead, which is read as “greater than or equal to”, makes 5 pass. A value that sits exactly where a test changes its answer is called a **boundary value**, and the figure shows what each version of the test does with it.

afterFigure.text: The two tests agree about every other value: 3 and 4 fail both of them, and 6 and 7 pass both. **They differ only at the boundary value**, which is why it is the value most worth checking when you follow a program. The symbol < is the mirror image of >, meaning “less than” and again leaving out equality, and <= is the mirror image of >=.

diagram.alt: Five circles for x equal to 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, each marked true or false for a test. With the test x > 5, the circle for 5 is false. With x >= 5 it is true. The other four do not change.
diagram.caption: The two tests agree everywhere except at 5, the boundary value. Use the buttons to switch the test.

lead.text: Work out the answer to the [[condition|A test with a true or false answer. Met earlier in this lesson.]] first, and then follow only the branch that it chooses.

reveal.text: Run the code above to compare: the test line appears once in the trace, and a single assignment follows it.

steps.headline: Trace x = 4 followed by: if x >= 4, add 10, otherwise subtract 1.

workedSteps.text: Line 2 is the test, and it is worked out with the value now stored in x.
The condition is true, so the first branch runs and the else branch is skipped.
No lines remain, so x finishes at 14.

steps.headline: Change the test in the earlier program to x >= 5, and trace it again from x = 5.

workedSteps.text: Line 1 stores 5 in x, as before.
The test is now x >= 5, and with the stored value it reads 5 >= 5, which is true, so the first branch runs.
The first branch adds 10 to the stored 5. Work out what x holds at the end.

steps.headline: A line written after an if/else runs on both paths, once the chosen branch has finished.

lead.text: In the programs so far the branches were the last lines. A line that is not indented, and so sits after the else branch, belongs to neither branch: it runs whichever path was taken, as soon as the chosen branch has finished. In the program below 7 >= 5 is true, the first branch makes x equal to 3, and the final line doubles it to 6.

afterFigure.text: The indentation is therefore doing real work. Move the last line four spaces to the right, so that it sits under else, and it would run only when the test was false, whereas left where it is it runs every time. This is the arrangement of the till rule, in which the tip was added to every bill whichever path the bill had taken.

lead.text: Follow this program, keeping in mind which of its lines belong to a [[branch|The indented lines that run only if the test is true, or only if it is false. Met earlier in this lesson.]] and which do not.

reveal.text: Had x started at 5, the first branch would have run instead, and the same final line would then have turned 15 into 30.

lead.text: A program is meant to add 10 when x is at least 3, and to subtract 2 otherwise. Run with x = 3, it takes the wrong branch, because its test leaves out the [[boundary value|A value exactly where a test changes its answer. Met earlier in this lesson.]].

reveal.text: The broken version finished at 1, because 3 > 3 is false and the else branch ran. Testing the boundary value first is the quickest way to find a fault of this kind.

lesson.orientation: Predict which branch of an if/else runs, and see why a boundary value matters.
lesson.nextAction: Say what makes a loop stop, and identify the change that would make it never stop.

blocks.text: A till program has to apply a rule such as this one: take £4 off any bill over £30, and add the tip afterwards. The £4 comes off only for *some* bills, so the rule is not a list of steps to be run one after another, and nothing in the first lesson could express it. The program has to put a question about the bill first, and let **the answer decide which path to follow**.
The figure follows two bills through the rule. Each takes one path only, and the two paths join again at the tip, which is added to every bill whichever path it took.

diagram.alt: A flow diagram of the till rule. A bill enters a test, over £30. Yes leads to take £4 off, no leads to leave the bill, and both paths meet at add the tip.
diagram.caption: Each bill follows one path only, and the paths meet again at the tip. Use the buttons to follow two bills.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say which branch of an if/else runs, including when a value sits exactly on the edge of the test.

recap.keyIdea: A condition is a true or false test, and it chooses one of two branches, so the symbol in the test matters most at its boundary value.

blocks.text: You followed programs in which the line if x > 5: sent x down one branch or the other, and saw that > and >= give *different* answers for exactly one value, the boundary. You also saw that a line placed after the else branch runs whichever branch was chosen.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson repeats lines for as long as a test stays true, which is how a program does the same work many times.

questions.prompt: Run the program. What is x at the end?
hints: Work out 5 > 5 before running either branch.
A strict greater-than comparison does not include equality.
Follow only the else branch when the condition is false.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 5 > 5 is false, so the else branch subtracts 1: 5 − 1 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: The test 5 > 5 is false, so only the else branch runs and the if branch is skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs the if branch. Check 5 > 5 first: is 5 greater than 5?
That is only the amount the if branch adds, and it would not run here.
One of the two branches always changes x. Which one runs?

questions.prompt: What is x at the end?
hints: The inclusive comparison is >= rather than >.
Test whether the stored 5 meets that condition.
Run the +10 branch only if the condition is true.
questions.onCorrect: With >= the boundary value takes the if branch, so one changed symbol changes the outcome.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the else branch. Is 5 greater than or equal to 5?
That is only the amount added. The if branch adds it to x.

questions.prompt: Run the program. What is x at the end?
hints: Run one branch, then continue after the if/else block.
For this input the else branch subtracts 1.
The later doubling still runs after the chosen branch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The else branch changes 2 to 1, then the final line doubles it to 2.

questions.onCorrect: The else branch made 1, and the last line runs on both paths, so it doubled that.

misconceptions.feedback: That is x after the branch. The last line still doubles it.
That runs the if branch. Does the starting value reach the threshold?

questions.prompt: Change the test to x >= 3. For input 3, what is x at the end?
hints: The repaired test includes 3.
Is 3 greater than or equal to 3? That picks the branch.
Apply that branch to the 3 you started with.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Using x >= 3 takes the first branch and gives 3 + 10 = 13.

questions.onCorrect: At the boundary, >= takes the if branch and adds 10. Test the exact threshold value first.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the broken version: 3 > 3 is false, so it subtracts 2.
That is only the amount the if branch adds. It adds it to x.

hints: The symbol > requires the left value to be larger than the right.
Compare equality with strict greater-than: they are different relations.
questions.onCorrect: False. 4 is not greater than 4: > leaves out equality, so equal values fail the test.

misconceptions.feedback: Strictly greater means more than. Is 4 more than 4?

questions.prompt: A program stores 8 in x. If x < 5 it subtracts 1, and otherwise it divides x by 2. What is x at the end?
hints: Work out 8 < 5 before changing x.
When that test is false, use the otherwise branch.
Divide the current 8 by 2, and do not also subtract 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 8 < 5 is false, so the other path gives 8 / 2 = 4.

questions.onCorrect: 8 < 5 is false, so the else branch halves 8 and the subtraction is skipped.

misconceptions.feedback: That runs both branches. Only one runs.

questions.prompt: A café takes £4 off any bill over £30. Your bill is exactly £30 and you add a £2 tip. How much do you pay in total, in pounds?
hints: Is a bill of exactly £30 over £30?
If it is not, does anything come off?
Add the tip to the full bill.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A bill of exactly £30 does not pass the test, so nothing comes off: £30 + £2 = £32.

questions.onCorrect: £32. “Over £30” leaves out £30 itself. A program makes the same choice, and has to be told which one it means.

misconceptions.feedback: The £4 comes off only for bills over £30. Is a bill of exactly £30 over £30?

questions.prompt: Why does the first branch run when x is 4?
hints: What does the = in >= allow?

acceptedIdeas: x >= 4 is true when x equals 4.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: x >= 4 is true when x equals 4.

choices.label: x >= 4 is true when x equals 4.
The if branch always runs first.

questions.onCorrect: The condition is true at the boundary because >= includes equality. That is the only difference from >.

misconceptions.feedback: Neither branch runs by default. The condition decides which one does.
4 is not greater than 4. The symbol is >=, not >.

questions.prompt: A program stores 6 in x. If x >= 6 it subtracts 1, and otherwise it adds 1. Then, on both paths, it doubles x. What is x at the end?
hints: Test 6 >= 6 before changing x.
Run only the branch it picks.
The doubling runs after either branch.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6 >= 6 is true, so x becomes 5. The last line doubles it to 10.

questions.onCorrect: The test picks one branch, then the line after the if/else runs on every path.

misconceptions.feedback: That takes the else branch. Is 6 greater than or equal to 6?
That is x after the branch. The last line still doubles it.

flashcards.front: Start x = 1. If x < 3, add 4; otherwise add 9. What is final x?
